q: Forty-eight hours after an open femur fracture, a 26-year-old man develops acute tachypnea, hypoxemia (SpO2 83%), acute confusion, and a pinpoint petechial rash across the anterior chest, axillae, and conjunctivae. What is the diagnosis?
e: The classic triad of Fat Embolism Syndrome (24–72 hr after long-bone/pelvic fracture) is respiratory distress/hypoxemia, neurological deterioration (confusion/agitation), and petechial rash on the chest/neck/axillae/conjunctivae. Early fracture stabilization and respiratory support are key.

q: A patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma arrives with sudden severe unilateral eye pain, colored halos around lights, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, and rock-hard globe. Which class of eye drops is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED?
e: Mydriatics/anticholinergics dilate the pupil further, bunching the peripheral iris into the trabecular meshwork and catastrophically worsening intraocular pressure in acute angle-closure glaucoma.

q: Which postoperative care position is recommended immediately after cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation?
o: Semi-Fowler's or lying on the NON-OPERATED side, avoiding coughing, straining, heavy lifting, or bending at the waist
Lying directly on the operated eye to apply pressure
e: Positioning on the unaffected side or supine/semi-Fowler's with a protective eye shield prevents external pressure and avoids intraocular pressure (IOP) spikes from Valsalva maneuvers.

q: While performing a subcutaneous injection of Enoxaparin (LMWH) in the abdomen (love handles), which two technique steps are specifically required?
o: Expel the manufacturer's air bubble and massage vigorously after injection
Do NOT expel the prefilled air-lock bubble, do NOT aspirate, inject into pinched abdominal fold at 90°, and do NOT massage afterward
Inject into the deltoid muscle at a 15° angle
e: Retaining the small prefilled air bubble ensures full dose delivery and seals the medication deep in subcutaneous tissue; avoiding aspiration and post-injection massage minimizes painful hematoma and ecchymosis.

q: Which angle of needle insertion is standard for Intradermal (ID), Subcutaneous (SC), and Intramuscular (IM) injections respectively?
e: Intradermal (e.g., Mantoux/BCG) = 10–15° bevel-up to raise a bleb/wheal; Subcutaneous = 45° (thin) or 90° (adequate tissue/insulin pen); Intramuscular = 90° perpendicular into deep muscle.

q: Which anatomical IM injection site is considered the SAFEST and preferred site for adults and children >7 months because it is free of major nerves and large blood vessels?
o: Ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius/minimus located by palm on greater trochanter, index on ASIS, middle toward iliac crest)
e: The Ventrogluteal site avoids the sciatic nerve and superior gluteal artery (hazards of the obsolete dorsogluteal site) and has a thin subcutaneous layer over thick muscle.

q: When administering ear drops (otic instillation) to a 2-year-old child versus an adult, in which direction should the nurse pull the pinna (auricle) to straighten the ear canal?
o: Up and back for both children and adults
Down and back for children <3 years; Up and back for adults and children >=3 years
Up and forward for children; down and forward for adults
e: In children under 3 years, the external auditory canal slants upward/shorter, so pull the pinna DOWN and BACK. In older children (>=3 yrs) and adults, pull UP and BACK.

q: A patient receiving Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) via a subclavian central line finishes the bag, and the next TPN bag from pharmacy is delayed by 45 minutes. Which fluid should the nurse temporarily infuse to prevent severe rebound hypoglycemia?
o: 10% Dextrose in Water (D10W) at the same hourly rate
Clamp the central line completely until TPN arrives
e: High-dextrose TPN stimulates high endogenous insulin secretion; abrupt cessation causes dangerous rebound hypoglycemia. Temporarily hang D10W at the identical infusion rate until the replacement TPN bag arrives.

q: What is the MAXIMUM permissible hang time for a single unit of Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs) from the time it leaves blood bank storage, to prevent bacterial proliferation?
e: A unit of PRBCs must be initiated within 30 minutes of leaving controlled blood bank refrigeration and completely infused within 4 hours maximum (infuse slowly at 2 mL/min during the first 15 minutes while observing closely for reactions).

q: Which IV fluid is the ONLY standard crystalloid compatible to run in the same Y-tubing alongside a Packed Red Blood Cell (PRBC) transfusion?
e: Only 0.9% Normal Saline is compatible with blood products. Dextrose solutions cause RBC hemolysis/clumping, and Ringer's Lactate contains calcium that chelates citrate anticoagulant and triggers microclots.

q: Which oxygen delivery device delivers the MOST precise, fixed FiO2 (24% to 60%) regardless of the patient's respiratory rate or tidal volume, making it ideal for COPD patients?
e: A Venturi mask uses color-coded precision jet nozzles (Bernoulli principle) to entrain fixed ratios of room air and oxygen, guaranteeing an accurate FiO2 (e.g., 24% Blue, 28% White, 31% Orange, 35% Yellow, 40% Red, 60% Green).

q: During a Mantoux (Tuberculin Skin Test / PPD) reading at 48–72 hours, which measurement determines a positive result?
o: Diameter of redness (erythema) measured in centimeters
Transverse diameter of palpable INDURATION (raised hardened area) measured in millimeters
e: Always palpate and measure ONLY the transverse diameter of induration (in mm), never erythema. Positive thresholds: >=5 mm (HIV, immunosuppressed, recent TB contact), >=10 mm (healthcare workers, high-burden regions/India), >=15 mm (no risk factors).

q: In a patient with an elevated central venous line air embolism (sudden dyspnea, chest pain, 'mill-wheel' heart murmur, hypotension), what is the immediate emergency patient position?
o: Left lateral Trendelenburg (Durant's) position — left side down with head lower than feet
e: Left lateral Trendelenburg (Durant's maneuver) traps the air bolus in the apex of the right atrium/ventricle, preventing it from obstructing the pulmonary artery outflow tract while giving 100% O2 and clamping the open catheter.

q: Which anticoagulant is SAFE to use throughout pregnancy for treating deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because it does NOT cross the placental barrier?
o: Low Molecular Weight Heparin (Enoxaparin) or Unfractionated Heparin
e: Heparin and LMWH are large negatively charged molecules that do not cross the placenta and are not secreted in breast milk, making them drugs of choice for DVT/PE in pregnancy (Warfarin is teratogenic in 1st trimester and causes fetal hemorrhage near term).

q: A patient taking Metformin for Type 2 Diabetes is scheduled for a contrast-enhanced CT angiogram. What is the key nursing protocol regarding Metformin and iodinated IV contrast?
o: Double the Metformin dose on the morning of CT
Hold Metformin at the time of or prior to iodinated contrast and withhold for 48 hours until renal function (eGFR/creatinine) is confirmed stable, to prevent lactic acidosis
Give Metformin IV during the scan
e: Contrast-induced nephropathy can impair renal clearance of Metformin, precipitating fatal Metformin-Associated Lactic Acidosis (MALA). Hold Metformin for 48 hours post-contrast and verify normal renal function before restarting.

q: Which class of antihypertensive drugs commonly produces a dry, persistent, non-productive cough due to accumulation of bradykinin and is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy?
e: ACE degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibitors elevate bradykinin (causing dry cough and rare angioedema) and cause fetal renal dysgenesis/oligohydramnios in pregnancy. Switching to an ARB (Losartan) resolves the cough (though ARBs are also contraindicated in pregnancy).

q: Which opioid overdose reversal agent has a shorter half-life (30–60 minutes) than most long-acting opioids, requiring close monitoring for recurrent respiratory depression ('renarcotization')?
e: Naloxone (competitive mu-opioid antagonist) reverses opioid respiratory depression within 1–2 min IV, but wears off in 30–60 min. Patients who overdosed on morphine, methadone, or oxycodone need continuous monitoring and repeat doses/infusion.

q: Which rapid-acting insulin analog can be administered immediately before (0–15 minutes prior to) a meal, with onset in 10–20 minutes and peak at 1–3 hours?
e: Rapid-acting analogs (Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine) act in 10–15 min (give with food tray present). Regular insulin acts in 30 min (the ONLY standard insulin for IV infusion in DKA). Glargine/Detemir are peakless 24-hr basal insulins (never mix in syringe).

q: A patient diagnosed with schizophrenia repeats verbatim every sentence spoken by the nurse during the mental status examination. Which speech/motor abnormality is this?
e: Echolalia = involuntary pathological repetition of another person's spoken words. Echopraxia = mimicking another person's physical movements. Neologism = inventing new private words.

q: A patient newly started on Risperidone suddenly develops painful upward deviation of the eyes (oculogyric crisis) and sustained twisting of the neck (torticollis). What acute extrapyramidal symptom is this and what is the rapid antidote?
o: Acute Dystonia; administer IM/IV Diphenhydramine or Benztropine/Promethazine
e: Acute dystonia (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, laryngospasm) occurs hours to days after starting antipsychotics due to sudden dopamine blockade and acetylcholine excess; it responds dramatically within minutes to IV/IM anticholinergics (Benztropine/Diphenhydramine).

q: Which neurotransmitter imbalance is most classically implicated in the positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) of schizophrenia (mesolimbic pathway)?
e: The dopamine hypothesis attributes positive psychotic symptoms to mesolimbic dopamine hyperactivity (blocked by D2 antagonists) and negative/cognitive symptoms to mesocortical dopamine hypofunction.

q: In Kübler-Ross's five stages of grief and dying, a patient newly told he has terminal cancer tells the nurse, 'If God lets me live until my daughter's wedding next year, I will donate half my savings to charity.' Which stage is this?
e: DABDA stages: Denial, Anger, Bargaining (attempting to negotiate/postpone death via promises), Depression, and Acceptance.

q: Which therapeutic communication technique is the nurse using when she says to an anxious preoperative patient, 'You seem very tense about tomorrow's surgery; would you like to talk about what worries you most?'
o: Making observations and offering broad openings / exploring
e: Making objective observations ('You seem tense') paired with an open-ended invitation validates emotion and invites the patient to express fears without imposing false reassurance ('Everything will be fine').

q: Where in the human brain is Broca's motor speech area located, injury to which produces non-fluent expressive aphasia with intact comprehension?
o: Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere
e: Broca's area (Brodmann 44/45, left inferior frontal gyrus) controls motor speech production (broken/telegraphic speech, intact comprehension). Wernicke's area (left superior temporal gyrus) governs language comprehension (fluent nonsensical speech).

q: Which valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle and has two cusps?
e: The Mitral (bicuspid) valve guards the left AV orifice, whereas the Tricuspid valve guards the right AV orifice; closure of AV valves creates the first heart sound (S1 'lub').

q: Which cells of the gastric mucosa secrete Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) and Intrinsic Factor essential for Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum?
e: Parietal cells secrete HCl and Intrinsic Factor (autoimmune destruction causes Pernicious Anemia). Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; G-cells secrete gastrin.

q: Which structure in the human respiratory tract serves as the primary anatomical site of alveolar gas exchange across the respiratory membrane?
o: Alveoli (Type I pneumocytes) and pulmonary capillaries
e: Type I alveolar pneumocytes form the ultra-thin blood-gas barrier for O2/CO2 diffusion, while Type II pneumocytes synthesize pulmonary surfactant to lower alveolar surface tension.

q: Which functional component of the nephron is the primary site of action for Loop Diuretics (Furosemide) via inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter?
o: Thick ascending limb of the Loop of Henle
e: Furosemide blocks the NKCC2 transporter in the thick ascending limb of the Loop of Henle, abolishing the medullary osmotic gradient and producing potent diuresis (with K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ excretion).

q: In hospital triage during a mass casualty disaster (START Triage system), which color tag is assigned to a conscious patient with a simple closed forearm fracture who can walk to the designated safe zone?
e: START triage colors: Red = Immediate life-threat (salvageable, e.g., tension pneumo/hemorrhage); Yellow = Delayed (serious, stable >1 hr); Green = Minor ('walking wounded'); Black = Deceased/Expectant.

q: Which ethical principle in nursing requires the nurse to tell the truth to patients and avoid deliberate deception?
e: Core bioethical principles: Autonomy (self-determination), Beneficence (doing good), Non-maleficence (do no harm), Justice (fairness), Fidelity (keeping promises/loyalty), and Veracity (truthfulness).

q: In inventory management of hospital pharmacy supplies, what does 'ABC analysis' classify items according to?
o: Vital, Essential, and Desirable clinical criticality (VED)
Annual usage consumption value (cost × volume: A = top ~70% value in ~10% items)
Alphabetical order of generic drug names
e: ABC analysis categorizes items by annual monetary expenditure (A = high value/low quantity, strict control; C = low value/high quantity), whereas VED analysis classifies by clinical criticality (Vital, Essential, Desirable).

q: What does the 'SBAR' standardized clinical handoff communication framework stand for?
e: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is WHO/Joint Commission's gold-standard structured handoff tool to minimize clinical communication errors during shift handover and physician escalation.

q: In statistical hypothesis testing, rejecting a TRUE null hypothesis (concluding an intervention works when it actually does not — false positive) is called:
e: Type I (alpha) error = false positive (rejecting a true H0, conventionally controlled at p < 0.05). Type II (beta) error = false negative (failing to reject a false H0; Power = 1 − beta).

q: An IV Heparin infusion is ordered at 1,200 units/hour. The pharmacy supplies 25,000 units of Heparin in 500 mL of D5W. What rate (mL/hr) must be programmed on the smart infusion pump?
e: Concentration = 25,000 units / 500 mL = 50 units/mL. Required rate = 1,200 units/hr ÷ 50 units/mL = 24 mL/hr.

q: In an examination with 100 questions (+1 for right, −1/3 for wrong), a candidate attempts 90 questions and gets 72 correct and 18 wrong. What is the candidate's net score?
e: Net score = Correct − (Wrong × 1/3) = 72 − (18 / 3) = 72 − 6 = 66 marks.

q: If all Nurses are Clinicians and some Clinicians are Researchers, which conclusion MUST logically follow?
e: Since all Nurses belong to the set of Clinicians, at least some members of the set of Clinicians are guaranteed to be Nurses. None of the statements establish an overlap between Nurses and Researchers.

q: Complete the analogy: Sphygmomanometer : Blood Pressure :: Spirometer : ?
e: A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure; a spirometer measures pulmonary lung volumes and airflow (FVC, FEV1).

q: Which Indian Nobel Laureate won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1968 for deciphering the genetic code and its function in protein synthesis?
e: Dr. Har Gobind Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (with Nirenberg and Holley) for interpreting the genetic code in protein synthesis.

q: Which cranial nerve carries parasympathetic efferent fibers supplying the heart, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract down to the splenic flexure of the colon?
e: CN X (Vagus nerve) provides ~75% of the body's parasympathetic innervation, slowing SA/AV node firing, constricting bronchioles, and stimulating GI peristalsis and secretions.

q: What is the normal resting tidal volume (TV) of a healthy 70 kg adult during quiet breathing?
e: Normal resting tidal volume is ~500 mL (~7 mL/kg IBW), of which ~150 mL fills anatomical dead space and ~350 mL participates in alveolar gas exchange. In ARDS, lung-protective ventilation uses 6 mL/kg IBW.

q: Which hormone secreted by the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney converts angiotensinogen into Angiotensin I in response to renal hypoperfusion or hyponatremia?
e: Juxtaglomerular cells release Renin upon low afferent arteriolar pressure, macula densa low NaCl delivery, or beta-1 sympathetic activation, initiating the RAAS cascade.

q: Where does physiological fertilization of the human ovum by a spermatozoon normally take place?
e: Fertilization normally occurs in the widest, longest segment of the fallopian tube—the Ampulla—within 12–24 hours after ovulation; implantation of the blastocyst occurs in the upper posterior uterine wall around days 6–7.

q: Which blood vessel carries OXYGENATED blood from the placenta directly into the fetal circulation (bypassing most of the fetal liver via the ductus venosus)?
e: Fetal umbilical cord contains 'AVA' (2 Arteries, 1 Vein): the single Umbilical Vein carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from placenta to fetus, while the 2 Umbilical Arteries return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

q: Which anatomical structure prevents food and liquids from entering the trachea during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
o: Epiglottis (folding posteriorly over the glottic inlet as the larynx elevates)
e: During deglutition, laryngeal elevation tilts the elastic-cartilage epiglottis down over the laryngeal inlet while vocal cords adduct, protecting the lower airway from aspiration.

q: In a standard ECG waveform, what electrical cardiac event does the QRS complex represent?
e: ECG waves: P wave = atrial depolarization; PR interval (0.12–0.20 s) = AV conduction; QRS complex (0.06–0.10 s) = ventricular depolarization; T wave = ventricular repolarization.

q: Which part of the brain contains the vital respiratory rhythm centers (pneumotaxic/apneustic and medullary DRG/VRG) and vasomotor cardiovascular control center?
e: The Medulla oblongata houses the primary respiratory rhythm generator, cardiac autonomic center, vasomotor center, and vomiting/cough/swallow reflexes, modulated by the Pons.

q: Which Gram-negative curved rod with darting motility produces cholera toxin that irreversibly activates Gs-protein/adenylate cyclase, causing massive 'rice-water' secretory diarrhea?
e: Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 secretes enterotoxin that elevates intracellular cAMP in enterocytes, driving massive Cl- and water efflux ('rice-water stools') without mucosal invasion; rapid ORS/RL rehydration is life-saving.

q: Which staining method is standard in NTEP microbiology laboratories to visualize acid-fast bacilli (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) in sputum smears?
o: Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) acid-fast stain (carbol fuchsin + 20% H2SO4 decolorizer + methylene blue)
e: Mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall resist acid-alcohol decolorization, appearing as bright pink/red beaded rods against a blue background on Ziehl-Neelsen staining (20% H2SO4 for M. tuberculosis; 5% H2SO4 for M. leprae).

q: What is the most common causative organism of uncomplicated community-acquired Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs) in women?
e: Uropathogenic E. coli accounts for ~75–85% of uncomplicated community-acquired UTIs via P-fimbriae adherence to uroepithelium.

q: Which disinfectant concentration of Sodium Hypochlorite (bleach) is recommended by WHO/AIIMS for disinfecting large hospital blood spills (>10 mL) and HIV/HBV contaminated surfaces?
o: 1% Sodium Hypochlorite (10,000 ppm) for large blood spills (0.5% / 5,000 ppm for general surface disinfection)
10% pure bleach poured directly on skin
e: 1% Sodium Hypochlorite (10,000 ppm available chlorine) with 10–20 minutes contact time is standard for large blood/body-fluid spills (absorb with disposable paper towels first, then disinfect); prepare freshly every 24 hours.

q: A patient taking broad-spectrum Clindamycin for 10 days develops foul-smelling watery diarrhea, fever, and leukocytosis (WBC 22,000) due to Clostridioides difficile colitis. Which hand hygiene rule is MANDATORY after caring for this patient?
o: Alcohol-based hand rub alone is sufficient
Hand washing with SOAP AND WATER (because alcohol does NOT kill C. difficile spores) plus Contact Precautions
e: C. difficile produces hardy bacterial spores resistant to alcohol hand rubs. Mechanical friction with soap and running water plus Contact Precautions (gown & gloves) and sporicidal (bleach) environmental cleaning are mandatory.

q: Which serological marker in a Hepatitis B panel indicates active viral replication and HIGH infectivity (e.g., high vertical mother-to-child transmission risk)?
e: HBeAg correlates strongly with high HBV DNA load and high infectivity. HBsAg = active infection (acute or chronic >6 mo); Anti-HBs = immunity (vaccine or recovery); Anti-HBc IgM = acute infection / window period.

q: Which hypersensitivity reaction type (Gell & Coombs classification) mediates acute IgE-driven penicillin anaphylaxis versus the Mantoux (tuberculin) skin test?
o: Type IV for anaphylaxis; Type I for Mantoux
Type I (Immediate IgE mast-cell degranulation) for anaphylaxis; Type IV (Delayed T-cell mediated) for Mantoux
Type III for anaphylaxis; Type II for Mantoux
e: Gell & Coombs: Type I = IgE anaphylaxis/asthma; Type II = cytotoxic IgG/IgM (hemolytic transfusion reaction, Rh incompatibility); Type III = immune complex (APSGN, SLE); Type IV = delayed T-cell mediated (Mantoux test, contact dermatitis).

q: Which high-level chemical sterilant/disinfectant (2% alkaline solution) is widely used in hospital endoscopy suites to reprocess heat-sensitive flexible fiberoptic endoscopes?
o: 2% Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) — 20 min for high-level disinfection, 10 hours for sterilization
e: 2% Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) and 0.55% Ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA) are standard high-level disinfectants for heat-labile endoscopes and cystoscopes; instruments must be thoroughly rinsed with sterile water afterward to prevent chemical colitis.

q: Which cardiac biomarker is the MOST specific and sensitive gold-standard laboratory indicator of acute myocardial cardiomyocyte necrosis?
o: High-sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I or T (hs-cTnI / hs-cTnT)
e: Cardiac Troponin I and T rise within 2–4 hours of MI onset, peak at 12–24 hours, remain elevated 7–14 days, and are exquisitely specific to myocardium (CK-MB returns to baseline in 48–72 hr, useful for detecting reinfarction).

q: What is the normal adult reference range for serum Potassium (K+), serum Sodium (Na+), and total serum Calcium (Ca2+)?
e: Core ICU electrolyte norms: Na+ 135–145 mEq/L, K+ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L, Cl- 98–106 mEq/L, Total Ca2+ 8.5–10.5 mg/dL (ionized 4.5–5.3 mg/dL), Mg2+ 1.7–2.2 mg/dL.

q: Which laboratory coagulation test monitors therapeutic Unfractionated Heparin versus oral Warfarin therapy respectively?
o: PT/INR monitors Heparin; aPTT monitors Warfarin
aPTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time — intrinsic pathway) monitors Heparin; PT/INR (extrinsic pathway) monitors Warfarin
e: Heparin prolongs the intrinsic pathway measured by aPTT (target 1.5–2.5× control), whereas Warfarin inhibits Vitamin K-dependent factors (especially short half-life Factor VII) measured by PT/INR (target 2.0–3.0; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valve).

q: In an adult patient with suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome or Heart Failure, a markedly elevated B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP >400 pg/mL) specifically reflects:
o: Increased ventricular myocardial wall stretch and volume overload (Heart Failure)
e: BNP and NT-proBNP are released by ventricular myocytes in response to volume expansion and pressure overload, helping rapidly differentiate cardiogenic dyspnea (heart failure) from pulmonary causes (COPD/asthma).

q: What is the classic '3 D's' clinical triad of Pellagra caused by severe Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency?
o: Dermatitis (Casal's necklace), Diarrhea, and Dementia (progressing to Death if untreated)
e: Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency causes Pellagra ('3 D's': photosensitive Dermatitis/Casal's necklace, Diarrhea, Dementia), classically seen in maize/jowar-staple diets low in bioavailable tryptophan/niacin.

q: Which ocular manifestation is the EARLIEST clinical sign of Vitamin A deficiency (Xerophthalmia) and what are Bitot's spots?
o: Corneal ulceration is earliest; Bitot's spots are retinal hemorrhages
Night blindness (XN) is the earliest symptom; Bitot's spots (X1B) are foamy triangular keratinized white plaques on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva
Cataract is earliest; Bitot's spots are eyelid cysts
Glaucoma is earliest; Bitot's spots are lens opacities
e: WHO Xerophthalmia stages: XN (night blindness — earliest symptom), X1A (conjunctival xerosis), X1B (Bitot's spots — foamy white plaques), X2 (corneal xerosis), X3A/B (keratomalacia), XS (corneal scar).

q: How many kilocalories (kcal) of energy are yielded per gram by Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats respectively?
e: Atwater physiological fuel values: Carbohydrates = 4 kcal/g, Proteins = 4 kcal/g, Lipids/Fats = 9 kcal/g (Alcohol = 7 kcal/g).

q: According to ICMR-NIN 2020/2024 dietary recommendations, how much additional daily dietary energy (kcal/day) is recommended during pregnancy (2nd & 3rd trimesters) and the first 6 months of lactation respectively?
o: +350 kcal/day in pregnancy; +600 kcal/day during first 6 months of lactation
+1,000 kcal/day in pregnancy; +100 kcal/day in lactation
e: ICMR-NIN recommends +350 kcal/day during pregnancy (2nd–3rd trimesters) and +600 kcal/day during 0–6 months of exclusive lactation (+520 kcal/day during 7–12 months).

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD Stage 4, not yet on dialysis) has serum potassium 5.6 mEq/L. Which food item should the nurse instruct the patient to STRICTLY LIMIT?
o: Bananas, tender coconut water, oranges, tomatoes, and potatoes
e: Bananas, coconut water, citrus juices, dried fruits, tomatoes, avocados, and potatoes are very rich in potassium and must be restricted in hyperkalemic CKD patients (leaching/double-boiling vegetables helps reduce K+ content).

q: Which sampling technique divides a hospital's nursing workforce into subgroups (ICU, ER, OBG, Ward) and then randomly selects nurses proportionally from each subgroup?
e: Stratified random sampling partitions the population into homogeneous strata (e.g., clinical units) and samples randomly within each stratum, ensuring proportional representation and reducing sampling error.

q: In a research study measuring blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer, the degree to which the instrument produces consistent, repeatable results across repeated trials is called:
e: Reliability = consistency/repeatability of measurement; Validity = accuracy (whether the tool truly measures the construct it intends to measure). A tool can be reliable without being valid, but cannot be valid unless reliable.

q: Which leadership style involves the nurse manager making all unit decisions unilaterally with strict command-and-control—generally suboptimal for daily morale, yet MOST effective during an acute Code Blue cardiac arrest or disaster?
e: Autocratic leadership provides rapid, unambiguous command during life-threatening emergencies (Code Blue, mass casualty), whereas Democratic/Transformational leadership fosters staff engagement and quality improvement in routine ward management.

q: In Donabedian's classic quality-of-care evaluation model, what are the three pillars used to audit nursing and hospital quality?
e: Donabedian's triad: Structure (facilities, nurse-patient ratios, equipment), Process (adherence to clinical bundles, hand hygiene, medication checks), and Outcome (CLABSI rate, pressure injury rate, mortality, patient satisfaction).

q: What is the recommended nurse-to-patient ratio in an Intensive Care Unit (ICU / Ventilated bed) per Indian Nursing Council (INC) / NABH accreditation norms?
o: 1:1 for ventilated ICU patients (1:2 for non-ventilated HDU/ICU)
e: NABH and INC norms mandate a 1:1 nurse-to-patient ratio for mechanically ventilated ICU patients (and 1:2 for non-ventilated ICU beds) on every shift to ensure safe hemodynamic and airway surveillance.

q: A patient with severe mitral stenosis develops atrial fibrillation. Which physical examination finding best differentiates an APICAL-RADIAL pulse deficit?
o: Radial pulse rate is faster than the apical pulse rate
Apical pulse rate (auscultated at 5th ICS left MCL) exceeds the simultaneously palpated radial pulse rate because weak contractions fail to transmit a peripheral pulse wave
e: A pulse deficit (Apical HR − Radial HR > 0) occurs in AFib or frequent PVCs when premature ventricular beats lack sufficient preload/stroke volume to generate a palpable radial pulse.

q: A patient presents with sudden tearing, ripping chest pain radiating directly to the interscapular back, BP 192/106 mmHg in the right arm vs 148/82 mmHg in the left arm, and a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray. What is the diagnosis and priority IV management?
o: Acute Aortic Dissection (Type A); immediately lower heart rate (<60 bpm) and systolic BP (<120 mmHg) with IV beta-blocker (Esmolol/Labetalol) BEFORE vasodilators, and prepare emergent cardiothoracic surgery
e: Tearing interscapular pain + >20 mmHg inter-arm BP differential + widened mediastinum = Acute Aortic Dissection. Always give IV beta-blocker FIRST (reduces dP/dt shear force) before adding Nicardipine/Nitroprusside to avoid reflex tachycardia.

q: A patient with pericardial effusion develops Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended jugular veins (JVD), along with pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in SBP on inspiration). What emergency procedure is life-saving?
o: Emergent pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration of pericardial fluid under echo guidance)
Rapid administration of IV Furosemide 80 mg
e: Beck's triad + pulsus paradoxus defines Cardiac Tamponade (obstructive shock). Urgent pericardiocentesis relieves intrapericardial pressure and restores ventricular diastolic filling; avoid aggressive diuretics/vasodilators that drop preload.

q: Which characteristic pain relief posture differentiates Acute Pericarditis from Acute Myocardial Infarction?
o: Pain worsens when leaning forward and improves when lying flat
Sharp pleuritic chest pain improves when sitting upright and leaning forward, and worsens when lying supine or taking a deep inspiration
Pain is exclusively relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin within 2 minutes
e: Pericarditis produces sharp, pleuritic retrosternal pain with a scratchy friction rub and diffuse concave-up ST elevations (with PR depression), classically relieved by sitting upright and leaning forward.

q: A patient with Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) of the left calf has swelling, warmth, and redness. Which routine nursing action is CONTRAINDICATED because it can dislodge the thrombus into the pulmonary circulation?
o: Vigorously massaging the affected calf or repeatedly eliciting Homans' sign
Elevating the leg gently as ordered
e: Never massage a DVT-affected limb or aggressively dorsiflex for Homans' sign (which has poor sensitivity/specificity and risks thrombus embolization -> pulmonary embolism).

q: What is the classic clinical triad of Ectopic Pregnancy prior to rupture?
o: Amenorrhea (6–8 weeks), unilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, and irregular vaginal spotting/bleeding
Painless profuse bleeding, soft uterus, and polyhydramnios
e: Any woman of reproductive age presenting with amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain, and vaginal spotting must be evaluated with urine/serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound to rule out ectopic pregnancy (most commonly ampullary tubal).

q: Which maneuver is used to deliver the placenta cleanly during Controlled Cord Traction (CCT) while preventing acute uterine inversion?
o: Pulling vigorously on the umbilical cord without abdominal support
Applying steady gentle downward cord traction ONLY during a uterine contraction while placing the other hand suprapubically to push the uterine fundus upward (Brandt-Andrews maneuver)
Pushing downward on the fundus aggressively while the uterus is relaxed
Inserting forceps into the uterine cavity
e: Brandt-Andrews counter-traction (pushing the contracted uterus upward above the pubic symphysis while applying gentle cord traction) delivers the separated placenta safely while preventing life-threatening acute uterine inversion.

q: In a term newborn undergoing phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice), which two nursing safety interventions are MANDATORY?
o: Apply heavy baby oil over the skin and keep eyes uncovered
Shield the infant's eyes with opaque eye patches (removed briefly during feeds for inspection/bonding) and cover the gonads while maximizing exposed skin surface, monitoring hydration and temperature
Keep the baby fully wrapped in blankets under the lamp
e: Phototherapy isomerizes unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble lumirubin. Mandatory care: opaque eye shields (prevent retinal damage), diaper over gonads, frequent repositioning, increased breastfeeding/hydration, NO oils/lotions (risk of thermal burns).

q: What is the physiological difference between Physiologic Jaundice and Pathologic Jaundice in a newborn?
o: Physiologic jaundice appears within the first 24 hours of life
Pathologic jaundice appears within the first 24 hours of life, rises >5 mg/dL/day, has total bilirubin >15 mg/dL in term infants, or involves direct bilirubin >2 mg/dL
Pathologic jaundice never occurs in ABO/Rh incompatibility
e: Physiologic jaundice appears AFTER 24 hours (typically days 2–3), peaks at days 3–5 (<12–15 mg/dL), and resolves by day 7–14. Any visible jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is ALWAYS pathologic (e.g., Rh/ABO hemolysis, G6PD, sepsis) and requires immediate workup.

q: Which symptom triad characterizes Wernicke's Encephalopathy caused by acute Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency in chronic alcohol use disorder?
o: Confusion/encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia), and gait ataxia
Manic flight of ideas, insomnia, and grandiosity
e: Wernicke's triad = Confusion + Ataxia + Ophthalmoplegia/Nystagmus (mnemonic: 'CAN of beer' -> Confusion, Ataxia, Nystagmus). Treat urgently with high-dose IV Thiamine BEFORE any dextrose to prevent irreversible Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation + amnesia).

q: Under India's National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) and the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, what key legal reform was enacted regarding attempted suicide (Section 309 IPC)?
o: Decriminalization of suicide attempts: any person attempting suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and must be provided mental health care and rehabilitation rather than prosecution
e: Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 presumes severe stress in anyone attempting suicide, decriminalizing it in effect and guaranteeing access to care, advance directives, and patient rights.

q: What is the target of the WHO/India '95-95-95' strategy under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) by 2025/2030?
o: 95% of hospitals having 95 beds and 95 nurses
95% of people living with HIV know their status, 95% of diagnosed receive sustained ART, and 95% on ART achieve viral suppression
e: The UNAIDS/NACP 95-95-95 targets aim to end AIDS as a public health threat: 95% diagnosed -> 95% on antiretroviral therapy (ART) -> 95% virally suppressed.

q: World Tuberculosis (TB) Day is observed every year on March 24 to mark Dr. Robert Koch's 1882 discovery of which organism?
e: On March 24, 1882, Dr. Robert Koch announced the discovery of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Koch's bacillus), commemorated annually as World TB Day.

q: Which Indian state was the first to achieve 100% primary literacy and consistently records the lowest Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) in India?
e: Kerala consistently leads India's SRS health indicators with the lowest IMR (~6 per 1,000 live births) and lowest MMR (~19 per 1,00,000 live births), along with high institutional delivery and literacy rates.

q: Who is known as the 'Father of Modern Immunology' for developing the world's first successful smallpox vaccine in 1796 using cowpox?
e: Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps with cowpox (vaccinia) in 1796, establishing vaccination and leading to global smallpox eradication (certified by WHO in May 1980).

q: Which universal blood donor group for Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs) lacks A, B, and Rh(D) surface antigens?
e: O Negative RBCs lack A, B, and D antigens (universal RBC donor for emergency uncrossmatched trauma transfusion), whereas AB Positive plasma lacks anti-A/anti-B antibodies (universal plasma donor).

q: A physician prescribes Gentamicin 1.5 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for an adult weighing 64 kg. The stock vial is labeled 80 mg per 2 mL. How many milliliters should the nurse draw up for ONE dose?
e: Single dose = 1.5 mg/kg × 64 kg = 96 mg. Stock concentration = 80 mg / 2 mL = 40 mg/mL. Volume = 96 mg ÷ 40 mg/mL = 2.4 mL.

q: An ICU fluid balance chart records 24-hour intake of 1,500 mL IV NS, 450 mL oral water, and 250 mL IV antibiotics; output is 1,650 mL urine and 150 mL surgical drain. What is the net 24-hour fluid balance?
e: Total Intake = 1500 + 450 + 250 = 2,200 mL. Total Output = 1650 + 150 = 1,800 mL. Net Balance = 2200 − 1800 = +400 mL.

q: A 24-hour hospital clock reads 14:40. What is the acute angle in degrees between the hour hand and the minute hand on an analog wall clock at 2:40 PM?
Arrange the following steps of the Nursing Process in their correct sequential order: (1) Planning (2) Evaluation (3) Assessment (4) Implementation (5) Diagnosis.
e: ADPIE sequence: Assessment (3) -> Diagnosis (5) -> Planning (1) -> Implementation (4) -> Evaluation (2).

q: A patient receiving IV Amiodarone for refractory ventricular tachycardia develops a prolonged QTc interval of 560 ms and runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia twisting around the isoelectric baseline (Torsades de Pointes). What is the FIRST-LINE IV medication?
o: IV Magnesium Sulfate 2 g over 5–15 minutes (and defibrillation if pulseless)
e: Magnesium Sulfate (1–2 g IV) stabilizes myocardial membrane excitability and terminates Torsades de Pointes even when serum magnesium is normal, alongside stopping QT-prolonging drugs and correcting K+ (>4.0 mEq/L).

q: An ER patient presents with narrow-complex regular Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) at 196 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, alert and oriented. After vagal maneuvers fail, how must IV Adenosine 6 mg be administered?
o: Rapid IV push over 1–2 seconds via a large proximal vein followed IMMEDIATELY by a rapid 20 mL Normal Saline flush (while on continuous ECG recording)
e: Adenosine has an ultra-short plasma half-life (<10 seconds). It must be given as a rapid IV bolus via the closest proximal IV port followed immediately by a fast 20 mL saline flush; warn the patient of a brief 5-second chest-flush/impending doom sensation.

q: Which clinical sign is elicited during abdominal examination of a patient with acute cholecystitis when the patient abruptly halts deep inspiration due to sharp RUQ pain under the examiner's palpating hand?
e: Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest during deep palpation below the right costal margin) occurs as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto the examiner's fingers, classic for acute cholecystitis.

q: A patient with liver cirrhosis and tense ascites undergoes large-volume therapeutic paracentesis (6 liters drained). Which IV colloid is infused to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (PPCD) and hepatorenal syndrome?
o: IV Human Albumin (6–8 g per liter of ascitic fluid removed when >5 L drained)
e: Draining >5 liters of ascites triggers splanchnic vasodilation and effective hypovolemia. Infusing 6–8 g of IV albumin per liter removed maintains intravascular oncotic pressure and prevents renal failure.

q: Which bedside maneuver immediately evaluates ulnar artery collateral blood flow to the hand BEFORE performing a radial arterial puncture for an ABG sample?
o: Modified Allen's test (flushing of palm within 5–15 seconds upon releasing ulnar pressure)
e: Modified Allen's test occludes both radial and ulnar arteries while the patient clenches the fist, then releases ONLY the ulnar artery; brisk return of palmar color (<5–10 sec) confirms patent collateral circulation so radial puncture is safe.

q: A patient with an acute basilar skull fracture exhibits bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), mastoid bruising ('Battle's sign'), and clear fluid dripping from the nose. Which bedside test confirms cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea, and what intervention is strictly contraindicated?
o: Halo/ring sign (and beta-2 transferrin/glucose positive); NEVER insert a nasogastric tube or pack the nose tightly
Dipstick protein only; insert an NG tube immediately
e: Clear nasal fluid forming a concentric yellowish 'halo/double-ring sign' on gauze (and positive glucose/beta-2 transferrin) indicates CSF leak through a fractured cribriform plate. Nasogastric/nasotracheal tubes are strictly contraindicated (risk of intracranial insertion and meningitis).

q: In a patient with suspected Pheochromocytoma (paroxysmal BP 230/130, palpitations, diaphoresis, headache), which two bedside nursing rules are CRITICAL?
o: Deeply palpate the abdomen every shift and give beta-blockers alone first
NEVER palpate the abdomen (can trigger lethal catecholamine surge) and ensure ALPHA-blockade (Phenoxybenzamine) is established BEFORE beta-blockade prior to adrenalectomy
e: Abdominal palpation of a pheochromocytoma can squeeze massive catecholamines into circulation, triggering fatal hypertensive crisis/arrhythmia. Preoperatively, alpha-blockade MUST precede beta-blockade to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

q: A patient with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is taught pursed-lip breathing. What is the exact physiological benefit of exhaling slowly through pursed lips?
o: Creates mild back-pressure (intrinsic PEEP) in small airways during expiration, preventing early bronchiolar collapse and reducing air trapping/hyperinflation
e: Pursed-lip breathing generates gentle positive expiratory airway pressure (~2–5 cmH2O), splinting floppy emphysematous airways open longer so trapped stale CO2-rich air can empty completely.

q: What is the classic clinical presentation of a patient with Cushing's Syndrome (chronic glucocorticoid excess)?
o: Weight loss, bronze hyperpigmentation, hypotension, and hyperkalemia
Central truncal obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, hyperglycemia, hypertension, and hypokalemia
Exophthalmos, heat intolerance, and weight loss
e: Chronic hypercortisolism (Cushing's) causes moon face, dorsocervical fat pad ('buffalo hump'), thin bruised skin with violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, and hypokalemic alkalosis.

q: A patient with Rheumatoid Arthritis differs clinically from Osteoarthritis primarily by exhibiting:
o: Asymmetric single-joint pain that worsens at the end of the day with <15 min morning stiffness
Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrists) with prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour) that improves with gentle movement, plus positive RF/anti-CCP
Exclusive involvement of DIP joints (Heberden's nodes)
Zero systemic fatigue or elevated ESR/CRP
e: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune synovitis affecting MCP/PIP/wrist joints symmetrically (sparing DIPs) with prolonged (>60 min) morning stiffness, swan-neck/boutonniere deformities, and elevated ESR/CRP/anti-CCP.

q: Which antidote is specifically administered for severe Benzodiazepine overdose (e.g., iatrogenic Midazolam respiratory depression during procedural sedation), and what is its key contraindication?
o: Flumazenil; contraindicated in patients with chronic benzodiazepine dependence or co-ingestion of tricyclic antidepressants (risk of intractable seizures)
e: Flumazenil competitively antagonizes the GABA-A benzodiazepine binding site. However, in chronic benzo users or TCA co-overdose it can precipitate refractory status epilepticus and arrhythmias.

q: A patient with acute iron tablet overdose arrives with severe vomiting, hematemesis, metabolic acidosis, and serum iron 480 mcg/dL. Which specific iron-chelating antidote turns urine a characteristic 'vin rosé' (pink-orange) color?
e: IV Deferoxamine binds free ferric iron to form water-soluble ferrioxamine, excreted renally with a classic 'vin rosé' pink-orange urine tint.

q: A patient exposed to benzocaine topical spray or dapsone develops central cyanosis unresponsive to 100% O2, chocolate-brown arterial blood, and pulse oximetry stuck at ~85% despite normal PaO2 on ABG. What is the condition and its antidote?
o: Methemoglobinemia; administer IV Methylene Blue (1–2 mg/kg)
e: Methemoglobin (Fe3+) cannot carry O2, causing 'chocolate-colored blood' and a classic saturation gap (SpO2 ~85% with high ABG PaO2). IV Methylene Blue (unless severe G6PD deficiency, where Vitamin C is used) rapidly reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+.

q: A patient starting IV Potassium Chloride (KCl) replacement for hypokalemia (K+ 2.6 mEq/L) has an order written as 'KCl 40 mEq IV push STAT.' What is the nurse's mandatory action?
o: Administer the 40 mEq IV push over 2 minutes

HOLD the order immediately and clarify with the physician—concentrated KCl must NEVER be given IV push (causes instant fatal cardiac arrest); it must always be diluted and infused via pump at <=10 mEq/hr peripherally (<=20 mEq/hr centrally on ECG monitor)
Give it IM into the ventrogluteal site
Inject directly into the arterial line
e: Concentrated KCl is a High-Alert Medication: IV push causes immediate lethal asystole/V-Fib. Always dilute thoroughly, use an infusion pump (max 10 mEq/hr peripheral; up to 20 mEq/hr central line with continuous telemetry), and verify adequate urine output (>=30 mL/hr).

q: Which adverse reaction is most characteristic of long-term Phenytoin therapy for epilepsy, requiring meticulous oral hygiene and regular dental follow-up?
o: Gingival hyperplasia (gum overgrowth), along with nystagmus/ataxia at toxic levels (>20 mcg/mL)
e: Phenytoin commonly causes gingival hyperplasia (prevented/minimized with soft brushing, flossing, folic acid, and dental care), hirsutism, osteomalacia, and cerebellar toxicity (nystagmus/ataxia) above therapeutic range (10–20 mcg/mL). IV Phenytoin must be diluted ONLY in 0.9% NS (precipitates in dextrose) and infused <=50 mg/min.

q: Which life-threatening adverse effect of Aminoglycoside antibiotics (Gentamicin, Amikacin, Streptomycin) requires monitoring trough drug levels and baseline renal/hearing function?
o: Nephrotoxicity (reversible acute tubular necrosis) and Ototoxicity (cochlear/vestibular CN VIII damage — often irreversible)
e: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent bactericidals with narrow therapeutic windows causing nephrotoxicity (monitor creatinine/urine output) and CN VIII ototoxicity (tinnitus, high-frequency hearing loss, vertigo).

q: Why should patients prescribed oral Alendronate (bisphosphonate for osteoporosis) take it first thing in the morning with a full glass of plain water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes?
o: To prevent severe pill-induced erosive esophagitis/esophageal ulceration and maximize poor oral bioavailability
e: Oral bisphosphonates cause caustic mucosal injury if lodged in the esophagus and bind calcium/food poorly; take on an empty stomach with 180–240 mL plain water and stay upright (sitting/standing) >=30 minutes before eating or lying down.

q: When preparing to administer an IV dose of Mannitol or Nitroglycerin or Amiodarone, which drug specifically absorbs into standard PVC plastic tubing and requires glass bottles or non-PVC (polyethylene) tubing?
e: Nitroglycerin (and IV Amiodarone >2 hr) leaches/adsorbs into standard PVC bags/tubing, losing up to 40–80% potency; infuse via glass bottles or specialized non-PVC tubing using a smart titration pump.

q: What is the normal volume of amniotic fluid at term (36–38 weeks), and what Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) thresholds define Oligohydramnios versus Polyhydramnios?
o: Normal ~800–1,000 mL; Oligohydramnios AFI <5 cm; Polyhydramnios AFI >24–25 cm
Normal ~100 mL; Oligohydramnios AFI <15 cm; Polyhydramnios AFI >50 cm
e: At term, normal amniotic fluid volume is ~800–1,000 mL (AFI 8–24 cm). AFI <5 cm = Oligohydramnios (associated with renal agenesis/Potter syndrome, IUGR, PROM); AFI >24–25 cm (>2,000 mL) = Polyhydramnios (maternal diabetes, esophageal atresia, anencephaly).

q: Which clinical sign in early pregnancy refers to bluish-violet discoloration of the vaginal mucosa and cervix due to increased pelvic vascularity around 6–8 weeks gestation?
o: Hegar's sign (softening of lower uterine segment/isthmus)
Osiander's sign (pulsation in lateral vaginal fornices)
e: Probable signs of pregnancy: Chadwick's = bluish-purple vagina/cervix; Goodell's = softened cervix ('like lips instead of nose tip'); Hegar's = softened uterine isthmus; Braxton Hicks = painless irregular contractions.

q: A laboring woman with severe mitral stenosis (NYHA Class III heart disease) enters the second stage of labor. Which obstetric strategy minimizes dangerous hemodynamic Valsalva spikes during delivery?
o: Encourage prolonged vigorous Valsalva bearing-down for 2 hours
Shorten the second stage using prophylactic outlet forceps or vacuum extraction under epidural analgesia, avoiding supine hypotension and Methylergometrine
Administer IV Ergometrine 0.5 mg immediately after delivery
Infuse 3 liters of rapid Normal Saline bolus
e: In maternal cardiac disease (especially mitral stenosis), avoiding Valsalva straining via assisted second stage (outlet forceps/vacuum), maintaining left lateral tilt, careful fluid balance, and AVOIDING Methylergometrine (causes severe vasoconstriction/pulmonary edema) are vital.

q: Which fetal presentation and position is the MOST common and favorable for spontaneous normal vaginal delivery?
o: Left Occiput Anterior (LOA) with vertex presentation
e: Vertex presentation in Left Occiput Anterior (LOA) position presents the smallest fetal skull AP diameter—the Suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm)—to the maternal pelvic inlet.

q: During a Non-Stress Test (NST) at 34 weeks gestation, what criteria define a 'REACTIVE' (reassuring) 20-minute fetal heart rate tracing?
o: Baseline FHR 180 bpm with zero accelerations
At least 2 fetal heart rate accelerations of >=15 bpm above baseline lasting >=15 seconds within a 20-minute window (normal baseline 110–160 bpm, moderate variability)
Flat baseline variability with sinusoidal oscillations
e: At >=32 weeks gestation, a Reactive NST requires >=2 FHR accelerations peaking >=15 bpm above baseline for >=15 seconds within 20 minutes (before 32 weeks, 10 bpm × 10 sec applies), confirming intact fetal autonomic oxygenation.

q: A newborn presents immediately after birth with excessive frothy white oral secretions, choking, coughing, and cyanosis on the very first attempt at feeding, and an attempt to pass an NG tube meets firm resistance at 10 cm with coiling on chest X-ray. What is the diagnosis and priority preoperative nursing care?
o: Cleft palate; feed rapidly with a wide nipple

Esophageal Atresia with Tracheoesophageal Fistula (EA/TEF); keep strictly NPO, elevate head 30–45°, apply continuous low-pressure suction to a Replogle tube in the upper blind pouch, and give IV fluids
Pyloric stenosis; give oral rehydration solution
e: The 3 C's (Coughing, Choking, Cyanosis) + frothy drooling + coiled NG tube = EA/TEF. Keep NPO, semi-upright (30–45°) to minimize gastric acid reflux through the distal fistula into the lungs, and maintain continuous low-suction pouch decompression.

q: Which clinical feature is a hallmark sign of Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) in an infant under 6 months of age (unlike pedal edema in adults)?
o: Tachypnea, diaphoresis of the scalp during feeding, poor feeding/easy fatigability, tachycardia (>160 bpm), and hepatomegaly
e: Infants with CHF classically show feeding intolerance/sweating while nursing, tachypnea with subcostal retractions, tachycardia, poor weight gain, and hepatomegaly (peripheral dependent edema is rare in young infants).

q: A 4-year-old child arrives with a bright-red, itchy vesicular rash appearing in successive crops ('dewdrop on a rose petal') with macules, papules, vesicles, and crusted scabs simultaneously on the trunk (centripetal distribution). When is the child no longer contagious?
o: 24 hours after the first vesicle appears
Once ALL skin lesions have completely dried and crusted over (scabbed), typically 5–7 days after rash onset
Immediately after fever drops on Day 1
e: Varicella (chickenpox) exhibits pleomorphic lesions (all stages simultaneously, centripetal on trunk/face) and requires Airborne + Contact precautions until every lesion has crusted/scabbed over.

q: Which oral micronutrient is given alongside low-osmolarity ORS for 14 days to all children aged 2 months to 5 years with acute watery diarrhea under WHO/GoI guidelines to reduce duration and prevent recurrence?
o: Oral Zinc (20 mg/day for >=6 months; 10 mg/day for 2–6 months) for 14 days
e: Zinc supplementation (10 mg/day for infants 2–6 mo; 20 mg/day for children 6 mo–5 yrs) for 14 days restores intestinal epithelial barrier integrity, shortens diarrheal episodes by ~25%, and reduces recurrences for 2–3 months.

q: In pediatric pain assessment, which validated observational behavioral scale (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability; scored 0–10) is most appropriate for a preverbal 14-month-old toddler?
e: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) is validated for infants/toddlers (2 months to 7 years) and non-verbal children; Wong-Baker FACES is used for ages >=3–4 years; Numeric 0–10 for >=7–8 years.

q: What is the correct compression depth and rate for high-quality Adult Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) according to AHA Basic Life Support (BLS) guidelines?
o: Depth at least 5 cm (2 inches) but not >6 cm (2.4 inches) at 100–120 compressions/min with full chest recoil and minimal interruptions
e: AHA Adult BLS high-quality CPR: Push hard (5–6 cm / 2–2.4 in), push fast (100–120/min), allow full chest recoil, minimize pauses (<10 sec), avoid hyperventilation (30:2 without advanced airway; 1 breath q6s with advanced airway).

q: Which pressure injury stage (NPIAP classification) presents as an intact localized area of non-blanchable erythema over a bony prominence (such as the sacrum or heel)?
o: Stage 2 Pressure Injury (partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis/blister)
e: NPIAP stages: Stage 1 = intact skin with non-blanchable erythema; Stage 2 = partial-thickness loss/shallow pink ulcer or serum blister; Stage 3 = full-thickness skin loss exposing adipose; Stage 4 = exposed bone, tendon, or muscle; Unstageable = obscured by slough/eschar.

q: What is the standard procedure for collecting a sterile midstream clean-catch urine specimen from an indwelling Foley catheter (closed drainage system) for culture and sensitivity?
o: Pour urine directly out of the bottom drainage collection bag
Clamp the drainage tubing distal to the sampling port for 15–30 min, scrub the needleless sampling port with 70% alcohol, and aspirate 5–10 mL using a sterile syringe
Disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing and catch drips
e: Never collect urine for culture from the drainage bag (stagnant, colonized with bacteria) and never break the closed system; always aspirate fresh urine aseptically from the designated needleless sampling port.

q: During a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) neurological assessment, a head-injured patient opens eyes only to painful pressure (E2), utters incomprehensible groaning sounds (V2), and exhibits abnormal decorticate flexion to pain (M3). What is the total GCS score?
e: GCS total = E(2) + V(2) + M(3) = 7. Remember 'GCS <= 8, Intubate' — a score of 7 indicates severe coma/brain injury with high risk of airway loss.

q: In India's Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016, amended), into which color-coded container must expired/discarded cytotoxic drugs and anatomical human tissue be segregated?
o: Yellow non-chlorinated plastic bag (for incineration / plasma pyrolysis / deep burial)
e: Yellow bag = human/animal anatomical waste, soiled cotton/dressings, expired/discarded medicines & cytotoxic drugs (cytotoxic labeled with 'C'), microbiology waste. Red = contaminated plastics; White = metal sharps; Blue = glassware/metallic implants.

q: A patient experiencing an acute Panic Attack in the ER hyperventilates rapidly, trembles, sweats, and screams, 'I'm having a heart attack and going to die!' What is the nurse's MOST effective immediate communication approach?
o: Leave the patient alone in a dark room to calm down
Stay calmly with the patient, speak in short, clear, simple sentences in a reassuring low tone, and guide slow diaphragmatic breathing
Give a detailed 15-minute lecture on cognitive distortions right away
Tell the patient sharply to stop exaggerating
e: During panic-level anxiety, perceptual field narrows dramatically and complex reasoning is impossible. Remain physically present for safety, reduce environmental stimuli, use short directive calm phrases, and coach slow breathing.

q: Which eating disorder is distinguished by dangerously low body weight (BMI <17.5–18.5 kg/m²), intense fear of weight gain, distorted body image, lanugo hair, amenorrhea, and bradycardia?
e: Anorexia nervosa features severe caloric restriction and dangerously low body weight with bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo, and risk of refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia) when nutrition is restarted.

q: A patient taking Sertraline (SSRI) starts an herbal supplement (St. John's Wort) and Linezolid, then presents with agitation, hyperreflexia, inducible ankle clonus, diaphoresis, tremor, and fever 39.4°C. Which drug emergency has occurred?
o: Serotonin Syndrome (hyperreflexia + clonus; stop serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines and Cyproheptadine)
e: Key exam differentiator: Serotonin Syndrome has rapid onset (<24 hr) with neuromuscular excitation (HYPERREFLEXIA and CLONUS), whereas NMS has slower onset with LEAD-PIPE RIGIDITY and hyporeflexia. Antidote for severe serotonin syndrome is Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist).

q: Under India's National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD, formerly NPCDCS), population-based screening for Hypertension, Diabetes, and three common cancers (Oral, Breast, Cervical) begins at what minimum age?
e: Under NP-NCD at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (HWCs), universal population-based screening via CBAC forms targets all individuals aged >=30 years for HTN, Diabetes, Oral, Breast, and Cervical cancers.

q: Which disease is the ONLY human infectious disease to have been completely ERADICATED globally through a coordinated vaccination campaign (declared eradicated by WHO in 1980)?
e: Smallpox (last natural case Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia, Oct 1977) was officially certified globally eradicated by the World Health Assembly on May 8, 1980 (Rinderpest is the only eradicated animal disease).

q: What is the definition of the 'Cold Chain' in immunization logistics, and which vaccine storage temperature range applies to most routine vaccines at a PHC Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR)?
o: A continuous system of storing and transporting vaccines at potent recommended temperatures from manufacturer to beneficiary; PHC ILRs maintain +2°C to +8°C
Storing vaccines in sunlight for activation
e: The Cold Chain preserves vaccine potency from factory to child's arm; at the PHC level, ILRs maintain +2°C to +8°C (with freeze-sensitive Pentavalent/HepB/IPV/Td placed in upper baskets and OPV/MR in lower baskets).

q: In a cohort study of 1,000 smokers (incidence of lung disease = 20 per 1,000) versus 1,000 non-smokers (incidence = 4 per 1,000), what is the Relative Risk (RR)?
e: Relative Risk (RR) = Incidence in Exposed / Incidence in Unexposed = 20 / 4 = 5.0 (smokers have a 5-fold higher risk of developing the disease). Attributable Risk (AR) = 20 − 4 = 16 per 1,000.

q: What is the toll-free national emergency medical ambulance number operating across most Indian states under the National Health Mission (NHM)?
o: 108 (and 102 specifically for Janani Shishu maternal-infant transport)
e: 108 is the integrated 24×7 emergency medical/trauma ambulance service, while 102 specifically provides free transport for pregnant women and sick newborns/infants under JSSK.

q: What does the 'ASHA' worker acronym stand for under India's National Rural Health Mission (NRHM/NHM)?
e: ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) is a trained female community health volunteer (1 per ~1,000 rural population) bridging the village community and public health services.

q: Which Indian scientist is celebrated for discovering the 'Raman Effect' in physics and became the first Asian to receive a Nobel Prize in Science (1930)?
e: Sir Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman discovered inelastic light scattering (Raman Effect) on February 28, 1928 (celebrated annually in India as National Science Day) and won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics.

q: What is the name of the statutory regulatory body in India responsible for establishing uniform standards of Nursing education (GNM, B.Sc., M.Sc. Nursing) across the country?
o: Indian Nursing Council (INC — established under INC Act 1947)
e: The Indian Nursing Council (INC), constituted under the INC Act of 1947 and headquartered in New Delhi, regulates nursing education standards nationally (with State Nursing Councils maintaining active nurse registries).

q: Which hormone secreted by the beta cells of the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas promotes cellular glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis (anabolic lowering of blood glucose)?
e: Pancreatic islet cells: Alpha = Glucagon (raises blood glucose), Beta = Insulin (lowers blood glucose via GLUT4 translocation & glycogenesis), Delta = Somatostatin (inhibits both).

q: Which blood cell component is primarily responsible for initiating primary hemostasis (adhesion and aggregation to form a temporary plug) at a site of vascular endothelial injury?
e: Platelets adhere to exposed subendothelial collagen via von Willebrand factor and aggregate via GPIIb/IIIa receptors to form the primary hemostatic plug, subsequently stabilized by the fibrin coagulation cascade.

q: A patient is prescribed 500 mL of 0.9% Normal Saline over 4 hours using a microdrip IV set (drop factor = 60 drops/mL). What is the drip rate in drops per minute?
e: With a microdrip set (60 gtt/mL), drops/min ALWAYS equals mL/hr! Rate = 500 mL / 4 hr = 125 mL/hr = 125 microdrops/min.

q: A hospital stockroom buys surgical masks at ₹400 per box and sells/bills them at ₹460 per box. What is the percentage markup (profit %)?
In a row of 35 nursing candidates waiting for document verification, Priya is 12th from the front. What is her position from the back of the row?
e: Position from back = (Total − Position from front) + 1 = (35 − 12) + 1 = 24th.

q: Find the missing letter pair in the alphabetical series: AZ, CX, EV, GT, ?
e: First letters advance by +2 (A, C, E, G -> I); second letters move backward by −2 (Z, X, V, T -> R). Hence the next pair is IR.
